questions.q: What is a token, roughly, for an English-language LLM?
options: A whole sentence
A chunk of about 3-4 characters — sometimes a word, sometimes a word fragment
Always exactly one character
Always exactly one whole word
questions.explain: A token is usually a few characters — a common whole word, a fragment of a longer word, or a punctuation mark — not a fixed unit like a character or a word.

questions.q: Why do modern LLMs use subword tokenization instead of a whole-word vocabulary?
options: A whole-word vocabulary would always run out — it can't represent every possible word, typo, or new term
Subwords are easier for humans to read
Whole-word vocabularies are too small to fit in memory
Subword tokenization was required by early internet browsers
questions.explain: A closed whole-word vocabulary will eventually hit text it has never seen. Subword tokenization (like BPE) can represent any string by falling back to smaller pieces or raw bytes.

questions.q: In the lesson's tokenizer demo, why did the same text produce 8 tokens under one tab and 10 under another?
options: The tool made a random error
The two tabs used different tokenizers — GPT-3.5/GPT-4's tokenizer vs. the older GPT-3 legacy tokenizer
One tab counted spaces as a character, the other didn't
The second tab translated the text into another language first
questions.explain: Tokenization isn't universal — each model generation has its own tokenizer, so identical text can produce a different token count depending on which one is used.

questions.q: What are LLM context windows and API pricing actually measured in?
options: Tokens, not words or characters
Words only
Lines of text
Paragraphs
questions.explain: Both context-window limits and per-request pricing are measured in tokens, which is why understanding tokenization matters practically, not just conceptually.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how does tokenization treat non-English languages and code compared to English?
options: Identically in every case
Non-English text and code generally split into more tokens per word than English, often costing more
Non-English text always uses fewer tokens
Code is never tokenized at all
questions.explain: Because tokenizer vocabularies are typically trained with a lot of English text, non-English languages and programming languages often split into more tokens per unit of meaning than English does.
